lesson.title: Fingerprints of Fire: Why Excited Atoms Glow in Specific Colors
lesson.summary: When atoms absorb energy and their electrons fall back to lower orbitals, they emit light only at specific wavelengths, producing a line spectrum that acts as a unique fingerprint for each element.
lesson.body:
The Bohr model describes an atom's electrons as occupying specific, quantized energy levels rather than any arbitrary distance from the nucleus. That single idea explains one of the oldest observations in chemistry: excited atoms do not glow with a smooth rainbow of colors, they glow with a small set of sharply defined lines. When an electron absorbs energy, from heat, electricity, or light, it jumps to a higher energy level. It cannot stay there indefinitely, and when it falls back down to a lower level, the atom emits a photon whose energy exactly equals the difference between the two levels, delta E = E_high - E_low. Because the energy levels themselves are discrete rather than continuous, only certain specific energy differences are possible, so only certain specific photon energies, and therefore only certain specific colors, can ever be emitted.

For hydrogen, the simplest atom with just one electron, these allowed wavelengths are predicted almost perfectly by the Rydberg formula: 1 / lambda = R (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2), where n1 and n2 are whole numbers labeling the lower and higher energy levels (n2 > n1), and R is the Rydberg constant, 1.097 x 10^7 per meter. Every electron transition that ends on the same lower level, n1, forms a family of lines called a series; the series ending on n1 = 2 happens to fall in the visible part of the spectrum and is called the Balmer series.

Take the transition from n2 = 3 down to n1 = 2. Plugging in: 1 / lambda = (1.097 x 10^7 m^-1)(1/4 - 1/9) = (1.097 x 10^7)(0.1389) = 1.524 x 10^6 m^-1, so lambda = 6.56 x 10^-7 m, or 656 nm, a deep red line known to spectroscopists as H-alpha. Using E = hc / lambda, that photon carries about 3.03 x 10^-19 J, or 1.89 eV. This exact red line is bright enough that astronomers use it to map clouds of hydrogen gas in distant nebulae, all thanks to the same electron transition happening in every hydrogen atom, everywhere in the universe.

Pass the light from an excited element through a prism or diffraction grating and, instead of a smooth rainbow, you see a pattern of sharp bright lines against a dark background, an emission spectrum. Because every element has a different number of electrons and a different set of allowed energy levels, every element produces its own unique pattern, as distinctive as a fingerprint. This is the chemistry behind flame tests: sodium ions produce an intense yellow line near 589 nm, the same emission that gives sodium vapor streetlights their characteristic color, while other elements produce entirely different sets of lines.

Elements with more electrons and more complicated energy level structures produce far more lines than hydrogen's simple series, but the underlying rule never changes: a line appears only where an allowed electron transition supplies a photon of exactly that energy. This same set of energy gaps, the very same lines, shows up again from the opposite direction in the next chapter, when we look at what happens when white light shines through a cool gas instead of a hot, glowing one.
